recent_works.title: A Shock‐Tube Study of the HCl + M → H + Cl + M (M = Ar) Rate Constant Using HCl Laser Absorption Near 3.3 µm
recent_works.abstract: ABSTRACT Hydrogen chlorine (HCl) is an important combustion intermediate during plastic (municipal waste) and composite propellant (aerospace) combustion, but the understanding of its high‐temperature chemistry is still evolving. In this study, the pyrolysis of 0.5% HCl in Ar was investigated behind reflected shock waves in a shock tube at temperatures ranging from 2290 to 3490 K and pressures from 0.7 to 3.6 atm. A laser source was set to access the R(8) transition line of H 35 Cl in the fundamental band near 3.3 µm at the specific wavelength of 3045.06 cm −1 . Numerical predictions using chemical kinetics mechanisms from the literature did not capture well the decomposition behavior of HCl in our conditions. According to these models, the most sensitive reaction HCl + M H + Cl + M (M = Ar) could be isolated, and its rate constant was retrieved from the experimental measurements. A pressure dependence was observed over the range of pressures covered. recent_works.title: Pyrolysis study of trimethyl phosphate: Impact of unimolecular decomposition reactions
recent_works.abstract: The pyrolysis of trimethyl phosphate (TMP), a fire-retardant candidate for lithium-ion battery electrolytes, was studied using a micro flow reactor with a controlled temperature profile (MFR) and a shock tube (ST). The kinetic data obtained allow for a better understanding of TMP chemistry and for model validation by covering low-to-high temperatures. TMP mole fraction profiles were obtained at 900–1200 K and 1 atm using the MFR combined with a quadrupole mass spectrometer, showing a TMP decomposition for temperature above 1000 K. CO time-history profiles were obtained using a ST with a laser absorption diagnostic during TMP pyrolysis at 1301–1695 K and near atmospheric pressure. CO time histories exhibited a gradual increase at low temperatures and a rapid increase at the beginning of the experiment, followed by a constant, slow growth at high temperatures. TMP chemical kinetic models from the literature underpredicted the TMP reactivity in both systems. Updating the TMP unimolecular decomposition reactions by including missing reactions improved the model prediction for both TMP and CO profiles, especially at the initial stage of TMP pyrolysis. recent_works.title: Laminar Flame Speed Measurements of a NH3/H2/N2 Natural Gas Surrogate at Elevated Pressures
recent_works.venue: Journal of Engineering for Gas Turbines and Power
recent_works.abstract: Abstract Ammonia is a promising carbon-free fuel alternative, offering higher energy density and easier storage compared to liquid hydrogen. This study presents experimental measurements of the laminar flame speed for an NH3:H2:N2 mixture with a 40:45:15 volume ratio at elevated pressures, contributing to the understanding of ammonia's potential for clean energy applications. Experiments were conducted using the Turbulent Flame Speed Vessel (TFSV) at Texas A&M University, employing high-speed schlieren photography to capture spherical flame propagation. Flame stretch effects were accounted for to determine unstretched laminar burning velocities over equivalence ratios ranging from 0.7 to 1.4 at pressures of 1 – 4 atm and an initial temperature of 293 K. At 1 and 2 atm, with air as the oxidizer, peak laminar flame speeds were 42.5 and 34.1 cm/s at ϕ = 1.1. Leaner mixtures at these conditions exhibited cellular instabilities. To mitigate these instabilities at 3 and 4 atm, the oxidizer was replaced with a 1:6 O2:He mixture, resulting in increased peak laminar flame speeds of 54.6 and 48.7 cm/s at ϕ = 1.1, respectively. recent_works.title: Assessment of detailed kinetics models for CO formation in ethylene combustion via time-resolved laser absorption
recent_works.abstract: The oxidation of C 2 H 4 was studied in a shock tube by tracking CO time histories using a laser absorption diagnostic in highly diluted mixtures. Experiments were conducted over a wide temperature range at near-atmospheric pressure for three equivalence ratios (ϕ = 0.5, 1.0, and 2.0). Key parameters related to CO formation timing and concentration were extracted from the time-resolved CO profiles. The results were compared with several modern detailed kinetics models from the literature revealing that, despite the many studies available on C 2 H 4 combustion chemistry, CO time histories can be used to further improve the next generation of model predictions of C 2 H 4 oxidation. Notably, the ranking of model performance based on absolute relative error was broadly consistent with findings from recent studies involving more diverse datasets and conditions. This work highlights the advantages of using species time histories—rather than relying solely on global metrics such as ignition delay times—for kinetics model validation and development.
